A rendőrség péntek délután egy holttestet talált a leégett terület átvizsgálása közben. Andrej Plenković horvát kormányfő és Zoran Milanović államfő is a helyszínre látogatott, írta az MTI. A spliti kórházban negyven embert láttak el, közülük heten lélegeztetőgépre kerültek. Eddig legalább 58 magyar állampolgárt kellett kimenekíteni a súlyos horvátországi erdőtűz érintette területekről – közölte a Facebookon Orbán Anita külügyminiszter a legfrissebb információk alapján. Két család, összesen hét magyar állampolgár csak gyalogosan tudott elmenekülni, és úgy tűnik, a járművük a tűzben maradhatott. Mintegy 45 főt egy sportcsarnokban helyeztek el, további 13 magyart pedig máshol, értük már elindult két kisbusz. A többiek ellátásáról a horvát hatóságok és a Vöröskereszt gondoskodik. https://www.politico.eu/article/document.text: BRUSSELS — The European Parliament will push for stricter limits on allowing oil and gas companies to be classed as green investments under the EU’s updated sustainable finance rules, according to a document obtained by POLITICO , The position will set up a fight with member countries, which want to loosen restrictions on fossil fuel companies under the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation — an EU law that aims to prevent greenwashing to support sustainable investment decisions. Under the SFDR’s new “transition” category — which covers companies that are switching from dirtier to cleaner business models — lawmakers state that fossil fuel companies should only be included if they invest more in green activities than in new fossil fuel projects over a three-year period. Advertisement Advertisement That would likely rule out French oil major TotalEnergies, for example, because it allocates 35 percent of its capital expenditure to new oil and gas activities, and only around one quarter to low-carbon energy. The European Commission’s initial proposal suggested a blanket exclusion of the fossil fuel industry, a tougher stance than the Parliament. Member countries propose the most lenient rules, agreeing in June that oil and gas companies could be included in the transition category if they spend one fifth of their capex on green activities, as defined under the EU taxonomy. MEPs in the economic committee will vote on the Parliament’s position on Sept. 10, before a plenary vote the following week. If approved, it will open the way for member countries and lawmakers to begin negotiations to reach a compromise. An overhaul of the SFDR was tabled by the Commission in November, following greenwashing concerns and complaints from fund managers about its complexity and costliness.

https://neweasterneurope.eu/2026/08/24/f.text: From social media to politics: Poland’s Ukraine debate Polish society’s relationship with Ukraine currently faces numerous problems. An early enthusiasm for aiding Ukrainians fleeing Russian aggression has often given way to anti-migrant sentiment. New thinking is needed in both Poland and Ukraine in order to maintain constructive bilateral links. August 24, 2026 - Anna Romandash Nata Yasevych - Articles and Commentary Photo: Shutterstock “The topic of Ukrainians’ presence in Poland has become very politically charged,” says Daryna Sydorenko, a senior advisor at the Alliance 24/08 NGO and coordinator for Observatory of Hate – See. Monitor. React., which monitors anti-Ukrainian hate speech, disinformation, and incidents of violence in Poland. She says that “What we have seen over the last few years is that the context of Ukrainians’ presence in Poland has changed very significantly. We have to take into account the political component.” Sydorenko’s project monitors Polish information space, looking for hostile narratives and tracing how they move between anonymous social media accounts, Telegram channels, politicians and mainstream media. The team also documents cases of violence and other incidents motivated by hostility toward Ukrainians. Its preliminary monitoring found a connection between the rise of hostile language on Polish-language Telegram and acts of aggression in the real world. “Over the last two years, on Facebook, TikTok, Telegram, and even already on LinkedIn, we saw a spike in negative comments about Ukrainians,” Sydorenko says. “These could be news stories about everyday conflicts that were heavily dramatized, or comments on political events.” The change in Poland’s attitude towards Ukrainians has been measurable. In the months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, support for receiving Ukrainian refugees was exceptionally high, standing at 94 per cent. But it has since declined. By July 2026, 52 per cent of Poles opposed accepting refugees from Ukraine, while 42 per cent still supported it. The decline does not mean that Polish society has turned against Ukraine. Opinions differ depending on the issue: refugees, military aid, trade, Ukraine’s EU membership and the country’s future borders all produce different responses. But the political space around Ukraine has become more contested, often expressed through disagreements over historical memory between two nations. Poland has a complex relationship with its eastern neighbour, especially over history after the First and Second World Wars. The most contentious subject is the violence in Volhynia, eastern Galicia and Chełm region, where many Ukrainians, Poles and Jews used to live alongside each other. Ukrainian insurgent forces carried out mass attacks against Polish civilians in 1943-45 that led to the deaths of up to a hundred thousand people. The killings were an organized effort at ethnic cleansing to prevent any Polish sovereignty over Ukrainian-majority areas claimed for a future Ukrainian state. Poles, including elements associated with the Home Army, carried out retaliatory attacks against Ukrainian civilians that resulted in the deaths up to twenty thousand people. Historians continue to debate the precise number of victims, classifications of genocide, chronology, extent of coordination by different organizations, and the broader political and wartime context. This tragedy that was once relatively removed from the public space in Poland, especially during communism, has become a major topic in Poland over the last decade. This follows the establishment of the July 11th National Day of Remembrance by parliament in 2016. For example, in 2008, only 20 per cent of Poles said they knew a lot about the Volhynia massacres, while 41 per cent said they had heard nothing about it. By 2023, 64 per cent said they were well informed and 92 per cent stated they knew about the events. That increase in awareness has coincided with a period in which the relationship between the two countries has been both unusually close and contentious. After February 2022, Poland became one of Ukraine’s principal supporters. Close to a million Ukrainian refugees are under temporary protection in Poland, while Polish society has provided extensive assistance. At the same time, disputes over grain imports, agriculture, refugee policy and military support began to enter both Polish and Ukrainian domestic politics. The historical dispute has also moved into a new phase. Poland and Ukraine have resumed cooperation on the search and exhumation of victims of wartime violence. In July 2026, Polish specialists began exhumations at the sites of the former villages of Ostrówki and Wola Ostrowiecka in Volhynia following the approval of Ukrainian authorities. For Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media analyst who studies disinformation, the existence of a historical dispute is not in itself evidence of manipulation. “Reliable debate always involves mutual listening, taking into account the opinions of both sides and considering new developments,” she says, “Its aim is not to attack or provoke hatred, but to explain issues and find agreement.” The problem, she says, is what happens when descriptions of historical atrocities are repeatedly placed next to negative stories about Ukrainians in today’s Poland. According to Mierzyńska, this historical component has become a part of a broader set of narratives aimed at reducing support for Ukraine. “One of the demands of [far-right] groups was the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres,” she says, “When the exhumations began, it turned out that they did not matter to them.” According to the expert, this indicates that even when there are attempts to address historical grievances, the political messaging remains unchanged. “Many posts are inflammatory and focus on descriptions of terrible crimes and torture that victims of the Volhynia massacres supposedly experienced,” Mierzyńska says. “Some contain false information. These posts are often published on social media and have been repeated for years.” She identifies several recurring themes: Ukrainians as a physical threat, the use of the Volhynia killings to make Poles fearful of Ukrainians, and claims that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory after the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian War. Earlier narratives focused more on competition for jobs, healthcare and places in schools and kindergartens. “Since the full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine, [these narratives] have been interwoven with current reports about crimes committed by Ukrainian citizens in Poland, with many of these being fake news,” the expert adds. “The most common narratives are intended to discourage people from helping Ukrainians,” she says. “Ukrainian refugees are blamed for problems that already exist in Poland.” The result, Mierzyńska says, is a particular kind of political message: the violence of the 1940s is presented as proof of how Ukrainians living in Poland behave in the 2020s. “Combining increasingly tense descriptions of historical atrocities with contemporary cases of law infringements creates strong fear, dislike and hatred toward Ukrainians,” she says. From history to the news feed The same pattern appears in Sydorenko’s monitoring of Polish-language Telegram channels. Telegram is not as widely used in Poland as Facebook or X, but she says it is useful because it aggregates material from other platforms and allows researchers to see which narratives and politicians are being promoted. “People who see themselves as being outside of the system use it,” she says, “They are looking for alternative information. They are not satisfied with the way news is presented by established, verified media, or they feel that those media outlets do not reflect their views.” “It is an unregulated space,” she says, “And precisely through such marginal routes, certain ideas can be pushed toward the centre. One of the most widespread ones was the danger posed by Ukrainians, the idea that Ukrainians are criminals and a threat to Poland.” One example concerned a cross-border operation against drug laboratories. The actual operation involved the Ukrainian and Polish authorities and laboratories in Ukraine, Poland and Moldova. But a version of the story was shared as evidence that Ukrainian criminal gangs were bringing drugs into Poland. “The news was presented as if it showed an influx of Ukrainian gangs into Poland,” Sydorenko says. “In reality, the news story was basically that Ukrainian and Polish services had closed a number of drug laboratories in a joint operation.” Other narratives are built around individual law infringements. Sydorenko says that even when there was a crime, it is often presented in a way that can give it a different meaning. Her team found cases in which Polish media highlighted a suspect’s Ukrainian nationality when it was not relevant to the story. In one case involving counterfeiters, two suspects were Polish, one Ukrainian and one Russian, but only the Ukrainian national was mentioned in the headline. “This does not comply with journalistic standards, to constantly indicate the nationality of a criminal,” Sydorenko says. “The Ukrainian then becomes associated with crime by himself. You may not even want to promote this narrative framework, but you select such stories disproportionately, and it begins to look as if this is actually the case.” The historical narratives operate alongside these stories. Sydorenko says her team has monitored claims that a “Banderite school” has been established in western Ukraine and that the ideology of Stepan Bandera – the leader of Ukraine’s nationalist movement during and after the Second World War – is spreading. These messages appear alongside discussions about the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), the Volhynia massacres and the ongoing exhumations. She says that “In one verbal attack on Ukrainian teenagers in Poland, the offender also used this language. He called them “Banderite children” and told them to go back to Ukraine.” In another case, a video showing a Ukrainian receiving a traffic fine was circulated on Telegram. Comments called for the person’s deportation. “The channels tried to create a picture where offences committed by Ukrainians prove a common characteristic,” Sydorenko says. “That they are arrogant, that they break Polish laws and that they abuse Polish hospitality.” How quickly online hatred spreads to verbal and even physical abuse was evident in Wrocław in July , where a Ukrainian couple was attacked in front of a convenience store for simply speaking Ukrainian. Sydorenko says the hostility is visible even under stories that have little to do with Ukraine’s government or the war itself. “The mentioning of Ukraine and Ukrainians is always accompanied by very strong emotions. For example, anger, aggression and irritation.” Her team has seen hundreds of negative comments appear beneath stories about relatively minor incidents involving Ukrainians. One example was a video of a person who had knocked over a rubbish bin, and who was allegedly Ukrainian. The incident was followed by comments calling for Ukrainians to be deported and argued that Poland had given them too much. “There were statements saying that we have given Ukrainians too much, and now they behave so ungratefully,” says Sydorenko. The role of Russia is important in spreading hatred toward Ukrainians on Polish social media. However, besides the many bots, a lot of the hateful narratives have been picked up by ordinary citizens with no connections to the Kremlin. “Researchers in Poland observe high activity by pro-Russian circles, Russian accounts and influencers on social media in these areas,” Mierzyńska says. “Very similar anti-Ukrainian content appears in parallel on Russian Telegram channels, sometimes in Russian state media, among pro-Russian activists in Poland and in far-right circles.” She adds that “It is also known that Russia benefits from the popularization of anti-Ukrainian content. Therefore, it is irrelevant whether the content is disseminated by Russian actors themselves, or whether they merely inspire specific groups in Poland, or perhaps – this should also be taken into account – some groups are simply paid to disseminate it. What matters is the effect.” Sydorenko describes a similar movement between platforms and political actors. She says some narratives begin in anonymous channels, are picked up by influencers or political figures and later appear in mainstream media. Even credible outlets can also strengthen a narrative without deliberately endorsing it, particularly through flashy headlines. “The media competition is very high,” she says. “They need to stay afloat with material that really attracts attention.” A neutral story can therefore fit into a hostile narrative simply through its presentation. “Nobody says that some stories should not be covered if they are important,” Sydorenko says. “But it is important to understand that, for example, the headline they pick can work in favour of [hatred].” Sydorenko argues that journalists have a particular responsibility because they can either interrupt or reinforce the process. “It is very important for journalists to monitor not only the Russian propaganda space, but also to make sure that they themselves do not become amplifiers of these thoughts, moods and frameworks.” For Mierzyńska, fact-checking alone will not solve the problem because the hate and fake news campaigns operate through repeated emotional exposure. “Cognitive operations primarily affect emotions,” she says, “The more often recipients encounter emotional reports on a particular subject, the more their way of thinking changes under their influence.” Her proposed response is less about another round of arguments over individual posts and more about the relationship between the two societies. “We cannot build resilience if we act only at the information level,” she says. “It is necessary to take care of good relations between Poles and Ukrainians. Integration, getting to know each other, and building trust are necessary.” “When [this happens], external influence will be of little significance. Both sides should work on this: Poles and Ukrainians, as well as the Ukrainian diaspora in Poland. This is what we need most today.” For Poland and Ukraine, the historical dispute is not going away. The Volhynia massacres remains a central part of Polish memory, and the search for all victims and their identification should continue – together with Ukrainian partners. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/1/.text: Listen (6 mins) Save Share Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why? on social media Share Add Al Jazeera on Google Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attends a plenary session as finance ministers and central bank governors from G20 countries meet in Asheville, North Carolina, on August 31, 2026 [Sam Wolfe/Reuters] By Usaid Siddiqui Published On 1 Sep 2026 1 Sep 2026 United States President Donald Trump’s administration appears to be taking steps to increase contact with key figures in Moscow, even as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and US-backed peace efforts remain stalled. The latest signs that the US wants to step up relations include a rare visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe and the surprise appearance of Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 meeting hosted by the US on Monday. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Ukraine’s Zelenskyy plans to hit Russia with ‘1,000 drones’ a day list 2 of 3 Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week list 3 of 3 Death toll from Russian strike on Ukrainian arms depot rises to 38 end of list However, this contact does not necessarily amount to a restoration of US-Russian relations, analysts said. Washington continues to back sanctions against Moscow while it wages war on Ukraine and major differences over territory remain unresolved. So what were these latest contacts about, and are US-Russian relations on the up? What US-Russian contact has there been in recent days? The most significant meeting recently was Ratcliffe’s visit last week to Moscow, where he held talks with Russian intelligence officials. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said President Vladimir Putin was informed about the discussions but did not personally meet Ratcliffe. Trump described the visit as “semiroutine” and said it was connected to efforts to end the war in Ukraine . US media reported that Ratcliffe also raised concerns about a possible Russian attack on NATO members and Russia’s relationship with Iran. Trump, who claimed he would end the Ukraine war within “24 hours” of starting his second presidential term in January 2025 but has since failed to broker an agreement, has generally sought to play down tensions between Washington and Moscow. After Ratcliffe’s visit, he said the CIA director had had “good talks” with Putin. “He’s not going to be attacking a NATO territory,” Trump said. Advertisement Despite that, Russia has warned recently that the United Kingdom could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory. “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which ⁠it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement in mid-August. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.” Separately, Siluanov made a surprise appearance at a G20 finance ministers meeting in the US state of North Carolina for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting. According to the Reuters news agency, Bessent made clear there would be no financial agreements or economic relief for Russia until the war ends. What is the latest on US-Russian talks on Ukraine? Hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak as neither side is willing to concede territory to the other. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks this year broke down chiefly over Moscow’s territorial demands. Moscow has demanded that Kyiv give up territory in eastern Ukraine while Kyiv has refused to surrender any land it still controls. (Al Jazeera) Last week, Ukraine’s top presidential adviser, Kyrylo Budanov, said talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US could be happening “very soon”. On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had held “detailed and constructive” discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about a possible visit to Ukraine and efforts to advance the peace process. In the meantime, the deadlock continues. Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange attacks, targeting each other’s energy infrastructure and fighting intense battles in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region. On Tuesday, Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured many more in Kyiv and surrounding areas, local authorities said. It was the sixth consecutive day of intense strikes on the capital. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelenskyy’s sanctions commissioner, told Reuters on Monday that he is due in the US capital on Tuesday on a trip that will include meetings with lawmakers. This residential building was damaged in a Russian attack on Kyiv on September 1, 2026 [AFP] Are US-Russian relations improving? If so, what does that mean? The restoration of high-level contacts between the US and Russia began earlier in Trump’s second term. Advertisement In February, Washington and Moscow agreed to re-establish high-level military-to-military talks, which were suspended just before the Russian war on Ukraine began. After the latest contacts, Keir Giles, an associate fellow of the Russia and Eurasia Programme at the think tank Chatham House, said evidence that “relations are being normalised between Washington and Moscow should deepen the sense of alarm”. “The US treating Russia as a partner not an adversary is a fundamental problem for all those countries that are under direct threat from Moscow – not just Ukraine but America’s European allies too,” Giles told Al Jazeera. Insiders have also warned that a rapprochement with Trump could further embolden Russia against NATO. In August after Moscow warned the UK of “consequences” for providing long-range missile components to Ukraine, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that these “consequences” could include the possibility of attacks. He said many military experts advising the Kremlin are convinced that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said. This week, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said he was unhappy to see Moscow represented at the G20 meeting on Monday. “We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” ⁠⁠he told Reuters. On Tuesday, European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis also said this is not the right moment to “normalise” Moscow’s participation in G20 gatherings. “I think the European position is known,” Dombrovskis told reporters on the sidelines of the North Carolina meeting.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqwy.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Dammam is the largest city in Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province By David Gritten Published 1 hour ago Two people were killed and eight others injured in an attack on an airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) says. Those killed at King Fahd International Airport were a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident, while the injured were Saudi, Indian, Yemeni, Bangladeshi and Nepalese nationals. The GACA did not say what type of attack occurred, but Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement has repeatedly targeted the kingdom's airports with drones and missiles. On Wednesday morning, two people were killed by debris from a drone that was intercepted over Eastern Province, where Dammam is located, the Saudi energy ministry said. The ministry said the drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybeh oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze. It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal. Another four drones were also intercepted on Wednesday night, according to the Saudi-led coalition that is supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but they have previously said they are attacking Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen. US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate Published 9 hours ago UK to deploy jets to defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks Published 1 day ago On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged Published 12 October At least 21 people have been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities. One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others â the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis' military spokesman said on Wednesday that they had targeted military equipment at an airport in the southern Yemeni city of al-Mukalla, which it said had been transported by Saudi Arabia for use by pro-government forces. Meanwhile, Houthi-run media reported that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours. According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago. The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period. The UN says more than 256,000 people have also been displaced. The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. Earlier this month, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a counter-offensive with Saudi air support. However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib, al-Jawf, Dhale and Shabwa provinces. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-sit-out-fi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OYSu The Under-15 World Cup has been met with some criticism, and not just because of Russia's participation Image: Patrick Reichardt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement With nearly 1,000 matches and 189 teams, the Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan is bloated even by FIFA's usual standards . It marks a change in its attitude to children's international tournaments, which have not existed on anywhere near this scale before. For Germany, it is too much too soon. The German FA (DFB) told DW that it had "consciously decided not to participate." The statement from the organization suggested the DFB — whose development of young players is under scrutiny after a run of poor performances by the men's national team — felt such a tournament was not appropriate for players so young. "At this age level, our identification and development process is still underway, and we therefore do not believe it is appropriate to nominate a fixed squad for an international tournament at this stage," it read. "More broadly, the DFB's approach to talent development is based on the principle of supporting young players in a long-term and age-appropriate manner. We carefully assess at which stage international competitions and development measures are beneficial for each age group. "In our view, young talents should not be exposed too early to the accompanying aspects of professional football. These include increased expectations and pressure, public evaluation of their performances, and early interest from agents and the football market." Germany remains cautious, with Moukoko an exception The refusal to play in the tournament, which began this week, is consistent with Germany's more cautious approach to youth development . While in some leagues, like the Premier League in England, there is no regulation about youths playing professionally, in Germany's top flight, the Bundesliga , players must be 16. In fact, before the 2020-21 season, players could not be granted a pro license before they were 17 years and six months old. That change enabled Youssoufa Moukoko to make his Bundesliga debut for Borussia Dortmund a day after his 16th birthday in 2020, becoming the league's youngest player in the process. Youssoufa Moukoko: Bundesliga's youngest-ever player To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video But, some would argue his is a cautionary tale. Hyped wildly due to his goalscoring exploits at youth level, Moukoko was fast-tracked by Dortmund and Germany, who called him up for the 2022 World Cup . Now, still just 21, he is struggling for game time and goals on loan at Corum, in the Turkish Super League, from Danish side Copenhagen. Players under 16 are also forbidden by FIFA from having an agent. But this is poorly regulated in some regions of the world. That led Bundesliga club St. Pauli, then in the second division, to announce they would no longer work with player agents or private agencies in their youth system in 2023. "We want to focus on partnership and dialogue with the players, their families and their relatives," explained the head of the club's youth academy, Benjamin Liedtke, as St. Pauli officially positioned themselves "against the commercialization of youth football." Germany not alone in declining invitation to tournament Germany are one of 22 nations to refuse the invitation to compete in the tournament, 18 of whom are from UEFA, Europe's confederation . The USA are also one of the prominent refusals alongside Ukraine , whose FA told German public broadcaster Sportschau that they initially refused on sporting grounds before claiming that "other countries indicated that they would compete but did not want to play against Russia." DW contacted a number of FAs to clarify this point but is yet to receive a response. FIFA President Gianni Infantino , who has become a notorious figure thanks to a number of scandals over the past year, told Sky in February : "We have to [look at reinstating Russia], definitely, because this ban has not achieved anything. It has just created frustration and hatred. Having girls and boys from Russia being able to play football games in other parts of Europe would help." Eight months later, he has his wish. The ongoing tournament, billed as the "FIFA U-15 World Cup & Festival" comprises eight-a-side games with 20 minute halves, a smaller pitch and a number of other technical tweaks. FIFA say the 2027 edition will be for girls teams only. "Young players need meaningful matches, different opponents and different football experiences in order to develop. Talent exists everywhere, but the opportunities available to young players are not always the same," said FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger, likely referencing that teams from Bhutan and Seychelles to the Bahamas and Vanuatu are present. "This tournament gives players from across the world the chance to compete, to learn and to grow." FIFA are yet to respond to a DW request for further comment. Some believe Arsène Wenger (left) is the man to replace Gianni Infantino as the head of FIFA Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance The round robin stage, according to FIFA, has placed teams in "groups that provide diverse sporting and regional representation" but also appears to have, at least initially, kept apart nations in conflict with each other. For example, Israel and Palestine or Kosovo and Serbia are not in the same groups but could, in theory, meet in the later stages of the tournament. This would not be allowed in senior football, thanks to various bans and workarounds. FIFA are vague about how the tournament works after the round robin, saying only that it will consist of "four to five additional matches per team, determined by results and subsequent tier placement. [There will be] one winner for each of the six tiers." It also said that the winner of the top tier will be crowned champions but all teams will play matches until the tournament concludes on October 30. But, given that they have been banned from international football since invading Ukraine in 2022 , it is the presence of a Russian national team at a FIFA tournament that will likely heap the most controversy on to young shoulders. Though a Russian presence was not the reason for German refusal, not attending for sporting reasons may also turn out to be a smart piece of sport politics. https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies.text: By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All October 18, 2026 2:10am Share on Facebook Share on X Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'What Belongs to Others' Courtesy of Warsaw International Film Festival Share on Facebook Share on X Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment The 42nd edition of the Warsaw International Film Festival is wrapping up on Sunday after its winners were unveiled during a Saturday night awards ceremony. The top honor, the Warsaw Grand Prix in the international competition of the Polish fest, went to Grzegorz Dębowski for What Belongs to Others . The film follows a Polish burglar who assumes the identity of a dead stranger’s girlfriend, with unexpected results. The jury said it awarded the top honor to the film “for its precise and delicate storytelling, its exceptional performances, and its complex portrait, devoid of judgment, of a flawed and elusive woman who undergoes a transformation as she slips into a stranger’s identity and life, and therein finds the possibility of her own.” Related Stories Music Macklemore Wraps Up Free Palestine Tour in London: "It Was More Uncomfortable for Me to Stay Silent" Movies 'Fuxi: Four Tales of Feasting' Review: Whimsical Chinese Film Explores Myth and History Through a Series of Tasty Treats The Warsaw best director award went to Chinese filmmaker Cai Chengjie for Suzhou Quartet , which the jury lauded as “an original and ambitious concept brought to life through striking cinematography and daring experimentation with narrative form.” The “visually captivating and richly layered meditation on life and mortality” tells the story of four people who meet by chance in a small noodle shop, only to find they are long-lost acquaintances. Meanwhile, the Warsaw festival also gave a special jury award to Maria Dębska for her performance in Through the Wall , directed by Maciej Sobieszczański, about two young political prisoners during the Stalinist terror in Poland who fall in love The jury lauded the actress for “a remarkably precise and emotionally truthful portrayal [and] for creating a complex character with great sensitivity and without exaggeration.” It added that the honor is also “for a role that stays with the audience long after the film ends.” Meanwhile, a special jury mention went to Bloody Men , directed by Jens Sjögren, with the jury saying it “captures with remarkable authenticity the chaos caused by domestic violence and the challenges faced by children growing up with a single parent struggling with personal difficulties and making decisions that repeatedly put the entire family’s safety at risk.” Also at Warsaw, the main award in the Competition 1–2 program, dedicated to directors’ first and second fiction features, went to Lorin Terezi’s Agia . “It is rare for a fiction feature debut to feel so complete,” the jury said. “Its structure recalls a Greek tragedy, offering a glimpse into a disappearing world. A subtle story of a young woman rebelling against patriarchal tradition and a world in which family honor is valued above life itself. Agia wants to live on her own terms and make her own decisions.” A special mention in the 1-2 program went to Urša Menart’s Everything That’s Wrong With You , “a touching portrait of a young woman desperately trying to find an honest human connection in a world full of emotional uncertainty, white lies and cheating German boyfriends.” The Warsaw documentary competition saw the award go to Jonas Spriestersbach’s Meanwhile in Namibia , which explores how the German government, instead of paying reparations for its occupation of Namibia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, offers development cooperation programs. “The director demonstrates an amazing ability to frame reality with extraordinary precision, letting the images slowly unfold and reveal the unsettling and absurd contradictions of human behavior,” the jury said. “The film addresses moral complexity without simple judgments, allowing viewers to construct their own meaning.” María Molina Peiró’s Like Any Other Mortal received a special mention in the doc program.
